title: Scalable and interoperable C-V2X framework for real-time intelligent decision support in autonomous mobility
summary: A modular, edge-intelligent mobility operating system (mOS) puts the intersection itself into the control loop: extensible JSON/Protobuf message sets replace rigid SAE J2735 binaries, and a mixed-reality testbed on the KAIST Munji campus lets a real autonomous vehicle negotiate with virtual cars and pedestrians in real time.

paragraphs: Cooperative-ITS research has mostly stopped at simulation or narrow testbeds, and the standardized binary message sets it relies on — SAE J2735, ETSI ITS-G5 — cannot be extended without breaking interoperability with devices already in the field. The road, meanwhile, still carries human-driven cars, pedestrians and micromobility that broadcast nothing at all, so a vehicle reasoning from connected data alone never sees the whole intersection.

This study proposes the mobility operating system (mOS): a plug-and-play, edge-intelligent framework in which the intersection interprets traffic and issues speed advice, validated on a mixed-reality testbed where a physical connected autonomous vehicle interacts with virtual agents in real time. Published in Communications in Transportation Research, with Prof. Inhi Kim as a corresponding author.

sections.heading: Infrastructure in the control loop
sections.body: Rather than making each vehicle smarter in isolation, mOS gives the intersection edge the deciding role. A reservation-based autonomous intersection management scheme (after Dresner and Stone) is extended so that the requesting vehicle's maximum speed is updated dynamically: the edge finds the space–time cell each approaching vehicle would occupy and returns a recommended speed for every timestamp. The vehicle's Apollo stack accepts the suggestion through ROS and CAN/BUS only when it poses no collision risk, so infrastructure guidance never overrides on-board safety.

sections.heading: Messages that can grow
sections.body: The message set is deliberately minimal — a mandatory timestamp plus application-specific fields, serialized as JSON or Protobuf — so new services can be added without renegotiating a binary schema. Transport is hybrid: gRPC carries compressed, field-name-free messages for time-critical commands that need acknowledgement, while RabbitMQ handles periodic best-effort data such as GPS updates. A Kubernetes-based system orchestrator monitors network and resource metrics, scales services horizontally when traffic surges, and lets neighbouring intersections hand over or offload computation instead of routing everything through a central cloud.

sections.heading: A testbed that is half virtual
sections.body: Experiments ran at a four-leg unsignalized intersection on the KAIST Munji campus in Daejeon, with 3.5 m lanes meeting the Euro NCAP recommendation and a controllable signal box switched off. The connected vehicle was a Hyundai Tucson Hybrid NX4 carrying a Novatel PwrPak7 GNSS receiver and an Epson G320 IMU (RTK-corrected, 100 Hz, 0.05 m deviation) plus a commercial 5G router. A metaverse server synchronizes virtual vehicles, a driving simulator and a pedestrian simulator into the same scene, so a person can step into the path of a real moving car with no physical risk.

images.caption: Components of the testbed: the CAV and its on-board modules, the Apollo autonomy stack, driving and pedestrian simulators, and the physical intersection paired with its mixed-reality counterpart where virtual vehicles are injected (Fig. 4, Oh et al. 2026, CC BY 4.0)

sections.heading: Guided crossings are smoother
sections.body: Two scenarios were compared with and without speed suggestions. Mean post-encroachment time (PET) fell from 5.99 s (SD 0.77) to 4.62 s (SD 1.10) for vehicle-to-vehicle interaction, and from 2.94 s (SD 0.93) to 1.76 s (SD 1.20) for vehicle-to-pedestrian interaction — shorter but also less variable gaps, indicating more predictable negotiation. Without guidance the vehicle read a jaywalking pedestrian as a hazard, braked abruptly and stopped mid-path; with guidance it crossed without stopping, while every guided PET stayed above the 1.0 s safety threshold.

images.caption: Speed profiles of the physical vehicle with (left, blue) and without (right, red) infrastructure speed suggestions, for V2V (top) and V2P (bottom) interactions — guidance removes the hard braking and full stop (Fig. 5, Oh et al. 2026, CC BY 4.0)

sections.heading: Real-time, with caveats
sections.body: Mean end-to-end latency was 48.46 ms (SD 63.62 ms, max 479.39 ms) and mean jitter 60.17 ms, with packet loss between 0.106% and 0.285% across approach speeds of 20–50 km/h — low enough for real-time speed advice, but with occasional spikes that would threaten safety-critical exchanges. The trials used a commercial 5G router rather than dedicated C-V2X infrastructure, so dedicated PC5 links should tighten these numbers; a head-to-head comparison against existing V2X systems and scaling across multiple intersections remain future work.

images.caption: Framework of mOS: the physical intersection, the system orchestrator (runtime observation → edge intelligence → re-configuration), the infrastructure intelligent system and the metaverse server that mirrors real vehicles into the virtual world (Fig. 1, Oh et al. 2026, CC BY 4.0)

title: Infrastructure-Assisted Safe Crosswalk Navigation for Autonomous Mobile Robots Using Isaac Sim and ROS2
summary: A delivery robot at a crosswalk cannot see what a fixed roadside camera can. This Isaac Sim–ROS2 pipeline lets a vision-language model read the intersection from infrastructure, combines that scene context with signal timing and Nav2's nominal velocity command, and has a hybrid safety layer decide whether to stop, wait, slow down or commit to crossing.

paragraphs: A robot waiting to cross a road is working with the worst possible viewpoint: low to the ground, easily occluded by a parked car or a waiting pedestrian, and with no way to know how much signal time is left. A camera mounted on the infrastructure above the intersection sees all of it. This project builds the pipeline that gets that view to the robot and turns it into a crossing decision.

A fixed infrastructure camera in Isaac Sim observes the intersection, and a vision-language model turns each frame into structured scene context — pedestrian behaviour, approaching vehicles, crosswalk occupancy, occlusion and blind spots, conflict risk, overall scene safety. That context is combined with signal phase and timing (SPaT) information and with the nominal velocity command Nav2 has already produced. A hybrid decision and safety node sits above Nav2 as a supervisory layer, validating or overriding the command before it reaches the robot.

The work is ongoing. Isaac Sim gives repeatable versions of the scenarios that are hardest to stage safely on a real street — night and backlight, an occluding vehicle, an occupied crosswalk, a turning vehicle, too little signal time left, and SPaT messages that arrive late or not at all.

sections.heading: Reading the intersection from infrastructure
sections.body: A fixed roadside camera covers pedestrians, vehicles, crosswalk occupancy and the regions the robot's own sensors cannot see. A vision-language model converts each observation into a structured scene description rather than a bare list of boxes, so the decision layer receives context it can reason about:
bullets: Pedestrian presence and crossing behaviour
Approaching vehicle movement
Crosswalk occupancy
Occlusion and blind spots
Conflict risk and overall scene safety

sections.heading: Is there time to finish crossing?
sections.body: Knowing the light is green is not enough — the robot has to finish before it changes. Crossing feasibility is evaluated from the signal side rather than assumed:
bullets: Current pedestrian signal phase
Remaining signal time and whether the signal data is still valid
Estimated robot crossing time
A safety buffer on top of that estimate

sections.heading: A safety layer above Nav2
sections.body: Scene context, signal context and Nav2's nominal /cmd_vel meet in a hybrid decision and safety module, which validates and modifies the command before it reaches the actuators. It resolves to one of six behaviours — stop, wait, slow down, proceed, commit to crossing, or emergency stop — so that a marginal or contradictory situation resolves conservatively instead of being left to the navigation stack.

sections.heading: Signal phase from the robot's own camera
sections.body: Alongside the simulation work, on-robot experiments test whether the pedestrian signal phase can be read directly from the robot's ZED2i camera at night, as a complement to SPaT messages. A stock YOLO11n detector using the COCO traffic-light class locks onto the vehicle signal head and reports RED — the wrong signal for a crossing robot. A model retrained on RED / GREEN / OFF pedestrian-signal classes picks out the pedestrian signal at the same crossing and returns pedestrian_green with about 0.9 confidence, at roughly 8 ms per frame on GPU. Both runs are in the Watch clips above.

sections.heading: Repeatable scenarios, measurable outcomes
sections.body: The pipeline is built as modular ROS2 (Humble) nodes so the same architecture can move to a real robot and real infrastructure cameras later. Five configurations are compared — vision-only, SPaT-only, infrastructure-VLM-only, infrastructure-VLM with SPaT, and the full hybrid with Nav2 — against crossing success rate, red-light violation rate, collision rate, unsafe entry rate, waiting and crossing time, decision stability, scene context accuracy and inference latency.

title: Audio-Visual Synergistic Role in Promoting Active Travel
summary: A multi-scale, explainable machine-learning framework using 2.79 million Shenzhen bikeshare trips shows that street soundscapes — not just streetscapes — shape cycling demand, with audio-visual synergies revealing high-leverage, low-cost design levers for active travel.

paragraphs: Cycling is central to sustainable, human-centric mobility, yet bikeshare usage stays low even where the macro-scale built environment is favorable. Drawing on 2.79 million dockless bikeshare trips in Shenzhen, China, this study asks whether the fine-grained things riders hear and see — soundscapes and streetscapes read from street-view imagery — also shape where people ride.

A multi-scale, explainable machine-learning framework (LightGBM with SHAP and Accumulated Local Effects) quantifies each dimension's contribution, its nonlinear thresholds, and the synergy between what a street sounds like and what it looks like.

sections.heading: Hearing the street, not just seeing it
sections.body: Earlier street-view studies quantified how a place looks — greenery, sky, perceived beauty — but ignored how it sounds. Eight soundscape indicators (intensity, quality, traffic/natural/mechanical sources, and pleasant-chaotic-eventful emotions) are derived alongside six streetscape indicators, then validated against on-site sound-level-meter readings at 72 points, reaching a moderately strong agreement (r = 0.60).

images.caption: Field validation of the soundscape: predicted sound intensity vs. on-site sound-level-meter readings at 72 sample points (r = 0.60), with the mobile audit setup — phone video plus a UT353 meter — shown at right

sections.heading: Sound outweighs sight
sections.body: Adding audio-visual perception lifts explained variance from R² = 0.40 (built environment only) to 0.60. The built environment still dominates (55.5%), but among the micro-scale cues the soundscape (24.7%) carries more weight than the visual streetscape (19.8%) — the first evidence that what riders hear can matter more than what they see. Natural sound, pleasantness, and sound quality are the strongest auditory drivers.

images.caption: Relative importance by group: distance to subway, population, and road-network centrality lead overall, while soundscape cues collectively outrank the visual streetscape

sections.heading: Effects that bend, not rise forever
sections.body: The explainable model reveals thresholds rather than straight lines. Cycling responds to subway access only within about 1 km, and bus density turns supportive past roughly 42 stops/km². Pleasant sound, sound quality, and natural sound help only up to a moderate level (≈ 0.5–0.6) and then reverse — pristine quiet often marks remote, low-demand areas.

sections.heading: When sound and sight work together
sections.body: The dimensions interact. High sound quality boosts cycling only where a street is not boring and also looks beautiful — quality alone is not enough. Natural sound and perceived safety reinforce each other strongly, creating calm, low-stress riding environments, though natural sound paired with visible affluence produces no such lift, since wealthier areas simply cycle less.

images.caption: Bivariate map of generalized soundscape vs. streetscape quality across Shenzhen (Spearman's ρ = 0.44): dashed pockets in southern Nanshan and Luohu score high on both dimensions, while most districts show an audio-visual mismatch

sections.heading: Design for the ear, not only the eye
sections.body: Because these sensory qualities are cheap to adjust relative to heavy infrastructure, they offer high-leverage levers: noise barriers and absorptive or vegetative screens, pleasant sound-masking, and safer, livelier street furniture. Planners should target places where audio and visual quality are mismatched, and tune each perception within its effective range rather than maximizing it.

images.caption: Bike-share usage across central Shenzhen: spatial density concentrated in Nanshan–Futian–Luohu (a), a twin-peaked daily rhythm around the AM and PM commutes (b), and an example origin–destination flow network (c)

title: Traffic demand modeling using agent model
summary: Building a digital twin of road traffic with agent-based simulation (2022~2025): macroscopic transport simulation is integrated with activity-based modeling to reproduce realistic traffic flows and predict traffic volumes at the micro-analysis-zone level.

paragraphs: A multi-scale simulation environment that mirrors the real transport system lets you analyse scenarios that would be difficult or impossible to test on the street — including mixed traffic where conventional and autonomous vehicles share the road. The platform is built to produce quantitative evidence for transport policy and decision-making.

Inside that environment, traffic demand modelling links aggregate travel-demand estimation to disaggregate, agent-based demand generation and then to network simulation. The aggregate stage estimates origin–destination flows at the MAZ (Micro Analysis Zone) level to capture the spatial pattern of travel; the disaggregate stage uses an activity-based model to represent individual activity and travel decisions at the person and location level. The result is one consistent chain from zonal travel patterns to individual activity plans to network-level flows.

sections.heading: Why go below the zone
sections.body: Traditional four-step models describe demand mainly at an aggregate or zonal level, which limits how well they can express complex, interacting decisions made by individuals. Data-driven approaches let higher-resolution mobility and contextual data carry the model, opening up how individual characteristics, activities, locations and transport conditions relate to the travel choices people actually make.

images.caption: The data-driven demand pipeline: population synthesis and activity scheduling from census, survey and spatial data, feeding MATSim

sections.heading: Generating the population, then its day
sections.body: Demand generation runs as two sequential generative stages, each formulated as a probabilistic process and each evaluated against empirical distributions:
bullets: A statistically representative synthetic population is generated by learning the joint distribution of observed population attributes from census and survey data
Conditional on that population, activity participation, timing, destination and travel mode are modelled jointly to produce each individual's activity schedule and the trips it implies
Generated individuals and activities are then assigned to real locations using available spatial information before their demand reaches the network

images.caption: The two generative stages — population synthesis, then activity scheduling — producing per-person daily schedules that become trip assignments

sections.heading: Checking the generated demand
sections.body: Activity schedules describe the sequence of activities and trips for every individual in the synthetic population. Those trips are converted into origin–destination demand at the location level and aggregated back up to MAZ level, where the generated pattern is compared with observed travel demand. The test is whether aggregate spatial and temporal travel patterns are reproduced while the individual activity plans underneath them are retained; only demand that passes is carried forward to network simulation.

images.caption: Generated versus observed origin–destination demand aggregated to MAZ level, compared by period

sections.heading: Simulating the network with MATSim
sections.body: The validated activity plans are simulated on the real road network in MATSim, an open-source agent-based framework where each individual plan is scored and revised through configured replanning strategies. Every agent starts from an activity plan and travels the routes connecting its scheduled activities; the collective movement produces network conditions, including congestion, that feed back into subsequent route and plan choices. Repeated simulation and replanning progressively stabilises both the plans and the network, yielding link-level and route-level volumes that can be compared with observation.

images.caption: The study network and the sections used for detailed comparison

sections.heading: Do the patterns look like a real day
sections.body: Outputs are visualised by time of day and trip purpose to see whether plausible temporal and behavioural patterns emerge. Classifying vehicle movements by activity purpose shows how the composition of demand shifts across the day: during the morning peak, volumes rise sharply and work trips make up a large share of travel, while in the off-peak afternoon work travel is increasingly mixed with other purposes. Quantitatively, simulated link-level volumes are compared against detector counts using the GEH statistic, which measures the discrepancy while accounting for the magnitude of flow.

images.caption: Simulated network flows by period — AM peak, non-peak and PM peak
Simulated link volumes compared with detector counts using the GEH statistic

sections.heading: Where it goes next
sections.body: Future scenarios can vary AV penetration rate, passenger-car-unit assumptions, multimodal interaction and supporting communication infrastructure, and can add dedicated AV facilities or AV-priority zones to alternative networks. The resulting route- and link-level demand can also feed downstream microscopic simulation when detailed vehicle interactions need evaluating — giving a controlled, reproducible way to compare transport policies and infrastructure strategies.

images.caption: The AV analysis module: penetration rate, passenger-car-unit, multimodal and infrastructure scenarios, and the handover to microscopic simulation
The integrated platform: a data hub feeding macroscopic and microscopic simulation, with analysis results returning to signal, infrastructure-guidance and transport-policy decisions
From the four-step model at zone level to an activity-based model at the individual level, and the traffic-demand scenario each produces

title: Real-time Prediction-based Conflict Measures for Evaluating Pedestrian Crossing Safety
summary: A unified prediction-driven pedestrian-vehicle safety evaluation approach for intelligent intersections, integrating deep learning-based behavior prediction with traffic conflict measures to evaluate pedestrian crossing risk in real time.

paragraphs: The overall objective is a unified prediction-driven pedestrian-vehicle safety evaluation approach for intelligent intersections. Deep learning-based behavior prediction is integrated with traffic conflict measures to enable real-time evaluation of potential and future pedestrian crossing risks across different intersection scenarios, from individual interactions to crowd crossings.

sections.heading: Deterministic conflict evaluation at non-signalized intersections
sections.body: Pedestrian and vehicle time-to-arrival are predicted with deterministic deep learning motion models, formulating the Predicted Lane-based Time-to-Collision (PLTTC) and benchmarking it against TTC, MTTC, and PET. Published in Transportation Research Interdisciplinary Perspectives (2025).

sections.heading: Probabilistic conflict evaluation under behavioral uncertainty
sections.body: Probabilistic trajectories generated with mixture-Gaussian model outputs yield the Stochastic Predicted Time-to-Collision (SPTTC) for early-stage conflict identification with high-variability pedestrian behavior. In revision at IEEE Transactions on Intelligent Transportation Systems.

sections.heading: Real-time crash risk at signalized intersections
sections.body: Deep learning-derived conflict information (Predicted Lane-based Gap Time) is integrated into Extreme Value Theory crash-risk estimation, comparing four EVT formulations against conventional conflict measures. In revision at Analytic Methods in Accident Research.

images.caption: Multi-camera trajectory data collection at a signalized intersection: camera positions, coverage, and views

sections.heading: Crowd crossing risk evaluation
sections.body: Collective pedestrian dynamics are learned with multi-agent trajectory prediction, and a Crowd Gap Time (C-GT) measure evaluates pedestrian-vehicle risk during crowd crossings against baselines such as the Social Force Model. Ongoing.

sections.heading: Behavioral validation with VR and EEG
sections.body: Virtual reality experiments with electroencephalography responses test whether prediction-based conflict measures reflect human-perceived crossing risk and can guide threshold calibration. Ongoing.

title: Human-centric traffic safety
summary: Investigating how drivers, pedestrians, and evacuees make decisions in safety-critical mobility situations through immersive VR experiments, covering micromobility safety, pedestrian-ADAS interaction, and underground/rail environments.

paragraphs: A long-running line of work using immersive VR experiments to measure how drivers, pedestrians, and evacuees actually decide, attend, and move in safety-critical mobility situations. Controlled virtual environments reproduce realistic urban roadways, school zones, tunnels, and subway stations while capturing behavior that would be unsafe or impossible to observe in the field.

sections.heading: Micromobility safety and driver behavior
sections.body: How a driver's own riding experience shapes overtaking maneuvers, lateral distance, and risk-taking around bicycles and e-scooters in mixed traffic, studied with VR-based driving simulators (Transportation Research Part F, 2026).

sections.heading: Pedestrian safety and ADAS
sections.body: How the presentation of safety information — a real-time count of crossing pedestrians, or a UWB-based pedestrian tag — changes braking behavior, cognitive load, and the safety margins drivers leave under uncertainty (Accident Analysis & Prevention, 2024).

sections.heading: Underground and rail safety
sections.body: VR studies of pedestrian evacuation route choice during subway-station fires, in-tunnel information design under varying lighting and speed limits (Tunnelling and Underground Space Technology, 2025), and how age-related perceptual constraints reshape transport disadvantage in railway information systems.

images.caption: Immersive VR experiment platform: Cyberith Virtualizer Elite 2 omnidirectional treadmill with HTC Vive Pro 2 and Unity 3D

title: Analysis Public Transport Accessibility
summary: A comparative framework that measures the gap between planned transit schedules (GTFS) and actual smart-card usage with an extended G2SFCA accessibility model, diagnosing where public transport supply and real travel demand diverge.

paragraphs: Many cities face a spatial mismatch where public transport supply is rigidly misaligned with real-world travel demand, leading to service inefficiency and transportation inequality. This research develops a comparative framework that analyzes the gap between planned transit schedules (GTFS) and actual passenger usage (smart-card OD data) with an extended spatial accessibility model, providing quantitative evidence of where transit resources are wasted or lacking — particularly during off-peak hours.

sections.heading: Extended G2SFCA methodology
sections.body: Diverse services are integrated into a single supply metric using gross floor area, and door-to-door accessibility combines walking and in-vehicle travel times with a Gaussian decay function — moving beyond binary catchment measurements toward a more realistic accessibility index.

images.caption: Analysis pipeline: data sources, preprocessing, accessibility calculation, and spatial analysis in ArcGIS Pro

sections.heading: Realization rate analysis
sections.body: GTFS supply and smart-card usage are matched at the stop level, and a regression-based realization rate quantifies how far the plan is implemented in reality: alignment is high during peak hours but efficiency drops significantly at midday.

images.caption: GWR local coefficients for planned supply vs. realized usage in Daejeon (AM / midday / PM)

sections.heading: Spatio-temporal mismatch
sections.body: Geographically Weighted Regression reveals a structural midday discrepancy near northern industrial areas of Daejeon — routes rigidly centered on commuting fail to serve midday lifestyle travel such as shopping and medical care — while western and eastern residential clusters use transit efficiently.

sections.heading: Policy implication
sections.body: Transit policy should align the destinations of supply and demand rather than simply increase supply volume, spatially reallocating surplus capacity from low-realization routes to active residential and commercial areas.

title: Remote Autonomous Driving: Tele-driving from Daejeon to Jeju and Naepo
summary: A live tele-driving demonstration controlling a driverless shuttle on Jeju Island from KAIST's Daejeon campus over 415 km, using ultra-low-latency network federated communication to relay live video and control commands without delay.

paragraphs: Fully autonomous driving still struggles with unexpected situations and complex road environments. Tele-driving offers a complementary alternative for the current transition period: a remote operator controls the vehicle in real time while retaining the ability to communicate with onboard passengers, enabling safer responses in unforeseen situations.

In 2025, TUPA and its collaborators demonstrated this at scale — remotely operating a driverless shuttle located on Jeju Island from the KAIST campus in Daejeon, a physical distance of 415 km. The work was carried out with Trento Systems, EMG and KAIST, combining wired and wireless network communication technologies based on KREONET for both external (vehicle-to-remote) and internal vehicle communication.
In 2026, the demonstration was repeated over a second route: a vehicle at the KAIST Mobility AX Research Institute in Naepo was operated remotely from the KAIST Munji campus in Daejeon.

sections.heading: Ultra-low-latency remote control
sections.body: Safe remote control of an autonomous vehicle requires ultra-precise software and real-time communication. The team's remote-control interface processes data in real time while maintaining stability, and an ultra-low-latency network carried live driving footage and control commands between Daejeon and Jeju without perceptible delay during real-world road testing.

sections.heading: Network federated technology
sections.body: For the first time, network federated technology was applied to remote driving, demonstrating seamless mobility communication across the wide-area link and bringing remote-controlled autonomous vehicles closer to everyday deployment.

sections.heading: Toward commercial services in restricted spaces
sections.body: If commercialized, tele-driving services are expected to first appear in limited, controlled spaces such as airports, ports, and logistics facilities, and as a mobility option for passengers with restricted destinations — part of a broader vision for mobility that is safer, smarter, and more human.

images.caption: System architecture: the simulator control module mapping steering, gear and door commands onto the remote cockpit; the video streaming module relaying the vehicle's camera feeds to the remote driver's view; and the KREONET wide-area link carrying both across the country
Preparing the driverless shuttle on Jeju Island ahead of the remote tele-driving demonstration from KAIST's Daejeon campus

title: Goal-Driven Experimental Pipeline for Multi-Vehicle Autonomous Driving in CARLA in ROS2
summary: A CARLA-ROS2 experimental pipeline for goal-driven autonomous driving on Lanelet2 maps, composing multi-vehicle scenarios that mix custom driving policies with rule-based autopilot vehicles to study interaction-aware driving behaviors.

paragraphs: Autonomous driving research increasingly emphasizes interaction among multiple vehicles rather than isolated ego-centric driving, yet controlled experiments mixing heterogeneous vehicle behaviors remain difficult without a unified, goal-driven experimental pipeline.

This research constructs a CARLA-ROS2 pipeline that enables goal-driven autonomous driving using Lanelet2 lane-level maps. Vehicles can be controlled either by custom driving policies or by CARLA's built-in autopilot, supporting flexible composition of multi-vehicle scenarios with varying ratios of autonomous and autopilot-driven vehicles — a foundation for studying interaction-aware driving behaviors, priority decision policies, and future V2X-based coordination.

sections.heading: Core capabilities
bullets: Lanelet2-based goal-driven driving experiments using lane-level map information
Multi-vehicle scenario composition with heterogeneous driving policies
Controlled evaluation of interaction-aware driving behavior under structured map and goal conditions
Modular ROS2 architecture enabling sim-to-real extension
Extensible toward V2X information sharing and priority-based decision policies, including learning-based policies (end-to-end, RL)

images.caption: End-to-end autonomous driving demonstration using CARLA-ROS2 integration, visualized in RViz alongside CARLA

title: Development of Industry-Specific Physical AI Foundation Models
summary: Generative AI has to leave the screen: an industry-specialised foundation model must perceive, reason, plan and act in a physical workplace. In this IITP programme led by Lotte Innovate, KAIST builds the humanoid side — simulation policy learning, VR teleoperation and Sim-to-Real transfer for a robot that has to hold up in a working logistics site.

paragraphs: Formally titled Development of Industry-Specific Physical AI Foundation Models and Cultivation of Next-Generation Convergence Talent, and run as the 2026 Generative AI Leading Talent Cultivation Program, this IITP programme runs from April 2026 to December 2029. Lotte Innovate leads the consortium; KAIST, Yonsei University and Inha University are the joint research organisations, and Lotte affiliates — Korea Seven, Lotte E&C, Lotte Global Logistics, Lotte World and others — provide the sites where the work is demonstrated and validated.

The premise is to carry generative AI past the digital domain of language and vision into the physical one: perception, reasoning, planning, action, operation. The technical goal of an industry-specialised Physical AI foundation model is deliberately paired with a talent track, which places students inside the affiliates so that the research and the industry feed each other.

sections.heading: Three universities, three layers
sections.body: Each partner owns one layer of the stack:
bullets: KAIST — core humanoid technology for next-generation logistics automation (generative AI + robotics)
Yonsei University — security- and policy-aware adaptive on-device–cloud optimisation for large-scale industrial edge computing
Inha University — MoE-robotics on-device vision-language navigation for facility management

sections.heading: KAIST's task: a logistics humanoid
sections.body: Four professors of the Cho Chun Shik Graduate School of Mobility take part, with Prof. Inhi Kim as the KAIST task lead. Four modules are developed in parallel and then integrated into a humanoid that can be deployed in a real logistics environment:
bullets: Module A — VLN: logistics navigation, task-aware network modelling and route optimisation
Module B — VLM/Vision: worker action observation, intent inference and collision avoidance
Module C — Sim-to-Real: simulation policy learning, VR teleoperation and real-robot transfer (Prof. Inhi Kim)
Module D — Integrated control: terrain-adaptive whole-body locomotion–manipulation and VLA-based control

images.caption: KAIST의 개요도 — the four modules developed in parallel (세부 1–4: navigation and route planning, whole-body control and locomotion, work understanding and intent inference, simulation and Sim-to-Real verification) converging on a Physical AI logistics humanoid

sections.heading: Four-year roadmap
sections.body: The work moves from simulation to a working site in stages:
bullets: Year 1 — foundation building: simulation platform, vision-language datasets and logistics network graphs, whole-body dynamics modelling
Year 2 — core models: domain-randomisation RL policy learning, VR teleoperation, VLM intent inference, VLA-based terrain-adaptive locomotion
Year 3 — robot integration: Sim-to-Real transfer experiments and gap analysis, teleoperation extended to real robots, integrated locomotion
Year 4 — integrated demonstration: field demonstration at Lotte logistics sites and generalisation on unseen terrain

images.caption: Phase 1 and Phase 2 of KAIST's task — foundation building and core model development, then real-robot integration and field demonstration
Consortium structure: three universities supply core technology and talent while Lotte Innovate leads and the affiliates host the demonstrations

title: VR Driving Simulator Platform
summary: An integrated platform combining VISSIM traffic microsimulation, a driving simulator, virtual reality, and Python to study connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic — the shared hardware and software base behind TUPA's human-in-the-loop driving studies.

paragraphs: TUPA develops an architecture that ties together VISSIM microsimulation, a physical driving simulator rig, virtual reality, and Python-based control and analysis code, so that vehicle dynamics, driver behavior, and surrounding traffic can all be represented within one framework.

The platform is the common foundation behind the lab's overtaking-behavior and metaverse co-simulation studies, and is intended to help develop and validate techniques for improving traffic congestion, safety, and network performance under connected and automated driving.

images.caption: PTV VISSIM traffic microsimulation linked to Unity, driven through a VR headset and a force-feedback wheel and pedal set

title: Metaverse-Based Emerging Technology: Unity–VISSIM Co-simulation
summary: A co-simulation environment linking PTV VISSIM's traffic microsimulation with a Unity 3D virtual environment, enabling human-in-the-loop testing with a VR headset and a force-feedback driving wheel and pedals.

paragraphs: Driver-in-the-loop experiments only work if the traffic model and the virtual world behave as one system. VISSIM computes the surrounding traffic — car-following, lane changing, signal control — while Unity renders the 3D road environment and the vehicle the participant is actually driving in VR. Coupling the two in real time gives a safe, repeatable testbed where a human driver interacts directly with dynamic virtual traffic.

sections.heading: Real-time bidirectional exchange
sections.body: Positions, speeds and signal indications computed in VISSIM are transmitted to Unity and rendered in the 3D scene. In the same loop, the participant's steering, acceleration and braking inputs are returned to VISSIM, where they change how surrounding traffic follows and changes lanes. The closed loop makes the human driver an active agent inside the traffic stream rather than a passive observer of a fixed visualisation.

images.caption: The same site in both engines — Unity's 3D road environment and the VISSIM network that drives the traffic in it

sections.heading: VR multi-agent driving simulator
sections.body: In the networked configuration several participants join the same virtual road network, each driving their own vehicle. Unity synchronises every participant's position and motion state in real time while VISSIM generates background traffic that reacts to all of them. That makes it possible to reproduce car-following, lane changes, overtaking, merging and unsignalised intersections — situations where one driver's decision changes the conditions everyone else faces — with synchronised trajectories and control inputs available for analysing interaction, conflict development and collision risk.

images.caption: The multi-agent laboratory in operation: Unity environment, VISSIM network, the physical rigs, and the driver's VR view
VR headset, force-feedback wheel and pedal set used for the driver-in-the-loop configuration

sections.heading: Where the platform is used
sections.body: Four application areas are the focus:

Automated–human vehicle interaction in merging, lane-changing, gap-acceptance and conflict-response scenarios

A complete experiment logs vehicle trajectories, steering and pedal inputs, signal states, interaction events and surrogate safety measures against synchronised timestamps — a common data layer that makes comparisons reproducible across human drivers, automated vehicles, infrastructure strategies and simulation versions.

title: Human Factor Safety: Interactive Driving Behavior in Overtaking Situations
summary: Using the multi-agent driving simulator platform, this line of work studies how a human driver negotiates overtaking maneuvers around a slower vehicle while oncoming traffic is present.

paragraphs: Overtaking is one of the highest-risk manoeuvres on the road: the driver has to judge oncoming traffic, closing speed and the slower vehicle's behaviour all at once. TUPA studies that interaction on its multi-agent driving simulator, which puts a human driver behind the wheel of the overtaking vehicle while other agents control the oncoming and low-speed vehicles.

The work spans several studies led by Dr. Taeho Oh — from overtaking manoeuvres on two-lane two-way roads, to how the safety of overtaking an e-scooter is judged differently depending on which vehicle you are in, to how road condition changes overtaking behaviour.

sections.heading: Two models for learning human judgment
sections.body: For the overtaking vehicle the task was posed as classification — distinguishing overtaking initiation, abortion, continuation and completion — while the oncoming vehicle was modelled as a regression on acceleration. The initiation dataset was severely imbalanced, with only 96 overtaking-initiation cases against 8,121 of normal driving, so SMOTE combined with Tomek links generated 7,909 synthetic samples. Training on the original data gave the higher raw accuracy (0.9859) but an F1-score of just 0.4941; the balanced set reached 0.9544 accuracy with an F1-score of 0.9548, a substantially better class-balanced result without overfitting. Among seven machine-learning algorithms Extra Trees ranked first on both tasks — about 0.95 accuracy and F1 for the overtaking model, R² of 0.77 and RMSE of 0.07 for the braking model — with XGBoost and Random Forest close behind at roughly 0.94.

images.caption: The overtaking scenario as modelled: relative distances and speeds between the subject vehicle, the slower lead vehicle and oncoming traffic, with time-to-collision
Two participants drive the same scenario from opposite roles — subject vehicle and oncoming vehicle — each with their own view

sections.heading: Perception of safety depends on what you are driving
sections.body: This study puts a participant on an e-scooter and has them overtaken by a vehicle they themselves drove earlier, without telling them. A Unity-based sequential simulation replays the overtaking manoeuvre each participant produced in the vehicle simulator while the same person now rides the e-scooter simulator. Ninety-three percent of respondents said they overtake safely, leaving sufficient distance — but only half of those felt safe while being overtaken on an e-scooter, and 64% reported feeling less safe from the e-scooter's perspective than from the driver's. Risk perception, in other words, depends on which road user you are.

images.caption: The sequential simulation process: a participant's own overtaking manoeuvre is recorded in the vehicle simulator, then replayed around them while they ride the e-scooter simulator, without their knowing it is their own driving
The 6-axis motion simulator and the e-scooter simulator used for the paired experiment

sections.heading: Driving safety according to road condition
sections.body: Micromobility fills the first and last mile, but infrastructure and regulation have not kept pace with how fast it spread, and being overtaken by a vehicle remains one of its sharpest safety problems. This study examines how cross-modal experience — a driver's own first-hand experience of riding micromobility — and road condition together shape overtaking behaviour towards e-scooters and bicycles. Drivers with cross-modal experience keep wider lateral clearances when overtaking both, and poor road surfaces make drivers widen clearance and fixate longer. The findings argue for educational programmes that build cross-modal experience and for targeted infrastructure such as dedicated e-scooter lanes.

title: Data-Driven Traffic Volume Imputation from Multi-Source Data Collection
summary: Combining Roadside Equipment (RSE) probe data with Vehicle Detection System (VDS) loop-detector counts, this research imputes and predicts traffic volume across a road network using graph-based deep learning — a practical, data-driven approach to real-world transportation operation.

paragraphs: Traffic detectors collect volume data so a city can see how its network is flowing — the basis for traffic management and for the information road users act on. In practice the record is full of holes: gaps open up hourly in the short term and, once a feed fails quietly, stretch out over months.

This work recovers the missing volume across a large urban network rather than at isolated detectors, using graph-based deep learning that reads the spatial and temporal dependencies between sensors. No single source covers the whole network on its own — roadside equipment (RSE) reports real-time speed, travel time and sample counts along road segments, while VDS loop detectors report volume, speed and occupancy at fixed points — so the two are fused on a graph representation of the road network.

sections.heading: Why a graph, and why two sources
sections.body: Representing the network as a graph lets information from observed locations support recovery where measurements are missing, and lets the model exploit recurring temporal patterns at daily, weekly and monthly scales at the same time. The central difficulty is heterogeneity: the sensing systems differ in spatial coverage, in the variables they measure, and in how they fail.

images.caption: The two data sources over the Daejeon network — RSE units reporting speed, travel time and sample counts along segments, VDS loop detectors reporting volume, speed and occupancy at points — and the daily, weekly and monthly periods the model reads them over

sections.heading: Attention-based spatio-temporal graph network
sections.body: Rather than treating detectors independently, the model learns dynamic spatial and temporal dependencies across the network. Stacked spatio-temporal blocks combine a self-attention sub-block with a graph convolution sub-block, giving a data-driven way to integrate heterogeneous observations and estimate traffic states where measurements are sparse or unavailable.

images.caption: Stacked spatio-temporal blocks, each pairing a self-attention sub-block with a graph convolution sub-block over the road network graph

sections.heading: Daejeon case study
sections.body: Applied to the city-wide traffic monitoring network in Daejeon, the framework recovered traffic volume with a mean absolute error below 12 vehicles per 5 minutes — evidence that multi-source sensing and graph-based learning can keep traffic information reliable even when a substantial share of the monitoring network is missing observations.

images.caption: Recovered versus observed flow at three detectors across several days, compared against baseline imputation methods

sections.heading: Reference
sections.body: Kwon, Donghyun, et al. Large-scale network imputation and prediction of traffic volume based on multi-source data collection system. Transportation Research Record 2677(9) (2023): 30–42.
